chapter_name: The Market as a Social Institution
learning_objective: 🎯 Understand how markets are not just about money and math, but are deeply embedded in social relationships, caste networks, and cultural practices!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: While economists view markets as spaces of rational calculation (Adam Smith's 'Invisible Hand'), sociologists argue that markets are socially embedded in relationships, trust, and community networks.
In India, trade was historically controlled by specific caste networks (like the Nattukottai Chettiars). Their business relied heavily on social trust and kinship ties (the 'Hundi' system).
A periodic market that serves as more than just a place to buy goods. It is a social gathering point for exchanging gossip, arranging marriages, and reinforcing social ties.
The process where things that were not traditionally bought and sold (like labor, organs, or even water) become commodities traded in the market.

fun_activity.title: 🛍️ The Local Haat Observation
fun_activity.instructions: Visit a local weekly market (haat/bazaar). Don't look at the products; look at the people. Notice how sellers group together, how people bargain based on familiarity, and how the market acts as a social meeting spot for friends.

exam_tips: 📌 Contrast Adam Smith's economic view ('Invisible Hand') with Karl Polanyi's sociological view ('social embeddedness').
📌 Use the Nattukottai Chettiars of Tamil Nadu as your primary example of how caste and kinship organize economic markets.
📌 Define commodification clearly and give a modern example (like bottled drinking water or surrogacy).
quick_recap: ⭐ Markets are created and maintained by society; they do not exist in a vacuum.
⭐ The colonial era connected local Indian markets to the global capitalist economy, changing them forever.
⭐ Globalisation has interconnected markets worldwide, bringing both new opportunities and new inequalities.
